chunks: What is RISC-V. The question: What is RISC-V?
RISC-V (said "risk five") is an open instruction set, a public rulebook for how a processor's instructions work.
Anyone can read it and build a chip that follows it without paying a license fee. It is a specification, not a chip.
It is also modular: a small base set of instructions, plus optional add-ons.
Imagine an open cookbook that anyone may cook from without paying.
The recipes are free, but ingredients, kitchens and chefs still cost money, and some kitchens turn out better dishes than others. RISC-V works the same way.
The rulebook is free, but designing, testing and manufacturing a chip are not, and chip quality varies a lot.
Fields are at fixed positions in R-type. In I-type the rs2 and funct7 fields merge into a 12-bit immediate, but rs1, rd and opcode stay put.
Fixed positions let hardware read the register file in parallel with decode.
ISA: the programmer-visible rulebook of instructions and registers ("What is an ISA?") Open: free to read and implement, with no fee to the ISA's owner.
Base ISA: the small required core, such as RV32I (32-bit integers). Extension: an optional add-on, such as M (multiply and divide) or C (shorter 16-bit instructions).
Core: one specific processor design that implements the ISA.
A name like rv32imc tells you what a core supports.
The 32 is the register width, the I means the base integer instructions, M means multiply and divide, and C means compressed instructions.
Software built for rv32imc will not necessarily run on a core that lacks M or C. Meanwhile, add x3, x1, x2 is the same 32-bit word, 0x002081B3, on every RISC-V core, tiny or huge.
That is the whole idea: one open rulebook with a base and optional parts.
"RISC-V is an open, royalty-free instruction set architecture, started at Berkeley and now run by RISC-V International.
It's a clean load/store RISC with fixed 32-bit instructions and 32 registers, built modularly: a small base like RV32I plus optional extensions such as M, F, C and V.
It's only the spec, not a chip, so anyone can build their own core."
